title: Tests with node:test

story: Nova keeps a status line in the ticket's Slack thread, and a small piece of the harness posts "Nova is on: build" through the broker whenever the step changes. Its first test called the real broker. So every CI run posted into the real RH-1234 thread, and by the afternoon the thread had forty copies of "Nova is on: plan" and a confused reviewer.

The test for the code that tags Nova's machine with its run id was worse. It needed real AWS credentials, CI has none, so someone marked it skip. A month later a typo in the tag name shipped, and the sweeper, the job that destroys machines left behind by finished runs, could no longer tell which machine belonged to which run.
hook.question: How do I test code that talks to Slack, GitHub or AWS without ever touching them, with nothing but the test runner that comes with Node?

p: In the frontend you use Vitest or Jest. Node ships its own runner, node:test, and an assertion module, node:assert/strict, so a platform package needs no test framework at all. A test is test("what should happen", fn): it passes when fn returns, or when the promise it returns resolves, without throwing. assert.equal compares like ===, and assert.deepEqual compares objects and arrays field by field.

To run TypeScript tests, Node loads tsx first with --import tsx, and --test takes a glob of test files. Put the glob in quotes, so Node expands it the same way on every machine instead of leaving it to your shell. Start with a pure function, one that only turns inputs into an output, because it needs nothing else.

notes.text: The strict module: equal means ===, and deepEqual compares deeply and strictly.
Tests import the source with a .js ending too, and tsx finds checkpoint.ts (lesson p1-1).
A model may write a step title with a newline in it. The commit subject keeps only the first line.

read.see:
$ node --import tsx --test "test/**/*.test.ts"
✔ a step becomes a wip commit message that skips CI (0.28ms)
✔ only the first line of a step title is used (0.04ms)
ℹ tests 2
ℹ pass 2
ℹ fail 0

read.h: Read the failure before you touch anything
p: When an assertion fails, the runner prints ✖ next to the test, then an AssertionError with the two values: + actual is what your code produced, - expected is what the test wanted. Below them is the file and line of the assert. The process exits with code 1, which is what makes CI red.

Read the two values first, because they usually tell you the whole story. Then decide which side is wrong. Most of the time it is the code. If the test itself was wrong, change it in a separate, explained commit, because a test that bends to fit the code no longer protects anything. That rule holds for agents too: the platform has a check that flags removed assertions and new skips in an agent's pull request.

read.h: Pass in what your code talks to
p: The Slack test went wrong because the reporter called the real broker by itself, so the test had no way to stop it. The fix is in the code, not in the test: the reporter receives the broker as a parameter. It asks only for what it uses, an object with a post method, and production passes the real broker client.

A test can then pass a fake: a stand-in that behaves like the real thing for this one purpose. mock.fn from node:test makes a fake function that does what you tell it and records every call, so the test can ask how many times it was called and with which arguments. No network, no Slack thread, and the test runs in under a millisecond.

notes.text: The reporter's whole view of the broker: one method. Anything with that shape will do.
The broker comes in from outside. The reporter never creates a client itself.
A fake post that does nothing and remembers every call.
Three reports, two posts: the repeated step was skipped.

deeper.h: Go deeper: testing a real server
p: Not everything should be faked. For the broker's own HTTP routes the test starts the real server, sends real fetch requests and checks the status codes, because callers depend on exactly those. The key is server.listen(0): port 0 asks the operating system for any free port, so several test files can run at the same time without fighting over 8080. before() starts the server once per file, and after() closes it, or the test process never exits.

The same idea as the fake broker works for time. A function that takes now as a parameter, with Date.now() as the default, can be tested at any moment you like, so a test about a five-minute timeout runs in a millisecond instead of five minutes.

The orchestrator talks to AWS through the AWS SDK version 3. There is one client per service, such as EC2Client for virtual machines, and every call is client.send(new SomeCommand(input)). Our tagging code takes the client as a parameter, like the reporter takes the broker.

The package aws-sdk-client-mock then replaces send on every EC2Client in the test process. You say what each command should return, or that it should fail, and afterwards you ask which commands were sent and with what input. No request leaves the laptop and no AWS account is needed, so the test runs in CI and nobody is tempted to skip it.

notes.text: From here on, every EC2Client in this process answers from the mock, never from AWS.
Forget earlier rules and recorded calls, so tests cannot leak into each other.
Every CreateTagsCommand that was sent, with its input.
Make the call fail, to test the error path without breaking anything real.
Passes only if the promise rejects with an error that matches the pattern.

lab.title: Eight tests, and none of them touches a real service
needs: About 60 MB of disk for the AWS SDK
lab.goal: Run node:test through tsx, read a failure, test the reporter with a fake broker and the tagging code with a mocked AWS client.

guess.q: The reporter is called with "plan", "plan" and then "build". The test passes a fake post made with mock.fn. What is post.mock.callCount()?

options.why: The reporter skips a step that is the same as the last one, so the second "plan" posts nothing.

options.text: 2, because the repeated step is skipped
options.why: "plan" posts, the second "plan" returns early, "build" posts. The fake recorded exactly what the real broker would have received.

options.text: 0, because a fake never really posts
options.why: The fake does nothing with the text, but it still counts every call. That record is what the test checks.

follow.say: Make the project with the AWS SDK for EC2, and the test tools: tsx and aws-sdk-client-mock.
follow.do: mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/p1-6/src ~/academy-labs/p1-6/test && cd ~/academy-labs/p1-6 && npm init -y > /dev/null && npm pkg set type=module && npm install --save-exact @aws-sdk/client-ec2@3.1150.0 > /dev/null && npm install -D --save-exact tsx@4.20.3 @types/node@24.12.2 aws-sdk-client-mock@4.1.0 > /dev/null && npm pkg set scripts.test='node --import tsx --test "test/**/*.test.ts"' && echo ready

lab.build: Write src/heartbeat.ts with isDead(lastHeartbeatAt, now = Date.now()): a machine is dead when it has been silent for more than five minutes, which is the rule the orchestrator uses for Nova's VM. Then write test/heartbeat.test.ts with three tests, all with fixed times and no waiting: a heartbeat 30 seconds ago is alive, exactly five minutes is still alive, and five minutes plus one millisecond is dead. npm test must show 8 passing tests.
checks: npm test ran the two checkpoint tests and showed ✔ for both.
Without the split, the second test showed + actual and - expected, and the exit code was 1.
The reporter test passed with a fake post, and nothing was sent anywhere.
Both tags tests passed with no AWS credentials on your machine.
After the build task, npm test shows ℹ tests 8 and ℹ pass 8.
lab.fix: A teammate made the heartbeat test "more realistic": it now waits five real minutes with await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 5 * 60_000)) and then calls isDead(last) with no now. CI takes five minutes longer, and the test fails on slow runners and passes on fast ones. Explain what went wrong, and bring back the fixed times by passing now in.
explain: Why did the fix for the forty Slack messages happen in the reporter's code and not in its test?
What does mockClient(EC2Client) replace, and why does the code under test stay exactly the code that runs in production?
When a test fails, which two values do you read first, and when is it right to change the test instead of the code?
lab.done: npm test shows 8 passing tests and exits 0, without network access to Slack or AWS.

check.q: The reporter creates its own broker client inside the function, and the test posts to the real Slack thread. What is the right fix?

options.text: Skip the test in CI and run it by hand before releases
options.why: A skipped test protects nothing, which is exactly how the tag typo shipped. The test should run everywhere, in milliseconds.

options.text: Let the reporter receive the broker as a parameter, so the test can pass a fake made with mock.fn
options.why: When the code receives what it talks to, production passes the real client and the test passes a fake. Nothing leaves the laptop.

options.text: Point the test at a separate Slack channel for tests
options.why: It still needs the network, a token in CI and a running Slack, and the test can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the code.

check.q: A test fails with + actual 'wip(RH-1234): Add the card\nand also rewrite the table [skip ci]' and - expected 'wip(RH-1234): Add the card [skip ci]'. What do you do first?

options.text: Change expected to the actual value so the test passes
options.why: That makes the test describe the bug. A test that bends to fit the code no longer protects anything.

options.text: Mark the test as skip until someone has time
options.why: A skip hides the failure from CI. The platform even flags new skips in agent pull requests.

options.text: Read the two values: the code kept the second line of the title, so fix the code to keep only the first
options.why: The two values tell the story. Here the test is right and the code forgot to cut the title at the first newline.

check.q: How does aws-sdk-client-mock let the tagging test run without an AWS account?

options.text: It starts a small local copy of AWS on your laptop
options.why: That is what tools like LocalStack do. aws-sdk-client-mock starts nothing; it works inside your test process.

options.text: It replaces send on every EC2Client in the process, so commands return what the test said and are recorded
options.why: The code under test is unchanged and still calls ec2.send. Only the answer comes from the mock instead of AWS.

options.text: It reads fake credentials from an environment file
options.why: With fake credentials the request would still go to AWS and fail. The mock stops the request before it leaves.

p: Every package in the platform repo tests with node:test and node:assert/strict, run through tsx with one root script: node --import tsx --test "*/test/**/*.test.ts". The broker's tests start from Byte's: a wrong capability gets 401, one repo cannot read another, and no token appears in any log. The gateway has a test that fails if any request text reaches its logs.

The orchestrator's activities are plain async functions on the AWS SDK v3, and the code that claims and tags a VM is tested with aws-sdk-client-mock. The checks around agent pull requests are tested the same way, with fixtures and node:test, and a separate check flags removed assertions, new skips and looser limits in an agent's change.

tickets.why: The root test script: node --import tsx --test over every package's test folder.
The broker's tests: wrong capability gets 401, no cross-repo reads, no token in any log.
The claim and tag code for VMs, unit-tested with aws-sdk-client-mock.
Flags weakened tests in agent pull requests: removed asserts, new skips, looser limits.

words.plain: The test runner built into Node: test(), mock and the --test flag.
Node's assertions where equal means === and deepEqual compares strictly, field by field.
A stand-in for something slow or outside, such as a broker or a clock, passed in by the test.
A fake function from node:test that records how often and with what it was called.
A library that replaces send on an AWS SDK client, so tests choose the answers and nothing reaches AWS.

review.q: From memory: the command that runs every TypeScript test in a folder, and why the glob is in quotes.
review.a: node --import tsx --test "test/**/*.test.ts". --import tsx lets Node load .ts files, and the quotes make Node expand the glob itself, the same on every shell and in CI.

review.q: You need to test a function that posts a Jira comment and then waits 30 seconds before checking a status. How do you make the test fast and offline?
review.a: Pass in the Jira client (or the broker) and the clock or sleep function. The test gives a mock.fn for the client and a fake clock or a sleep that returns at once, then checks the calls.

remember: Run tests with node --test through tsx, and pass in everything your code talks to, so every test uses a fake and never a real service.
